name: conceptual-contour
intent: Group the data, invariants and operations that belong to one domain concept into a single cohesive unit with a narrow domain interface, so the model's divisions follow the domain itself instead of technical convenience.
problem: Conceptually related behaviour is scattered: one concept's rules live across *Service classes, helper modules and utility functions, while an unrelated monolithic class or module mixes meanings, duplicates functionality and exposes an interface that does not say what clients actually need.
context: Any non-trivial domain model (DDD entities, value objects, aggregates, domain services, modules) where the model is being built or refactored: cutting a god class, de-anemizing entities, or deciding which operations, types and functions share a file, package or namespace. It presupposes that the domain can be named - a ubiquitous language and access to domain knowledge - because the contour is taken from the domain, not from the code layout.
benefits: Behaviour lives with the data it serves: invariants and rules are enforced in the one unit that owns the state, so callers cannot bypass them by reaching around the operation (the antidote to the anemic domain model).
Interfaces become the ubiquitous language: a small set of operations makes sensible domain statements instead of exposing every attribute, so clients and domain experts talk about the same things.
Changes localize: a rule change touches one cohesive unit instead of every service, helper and caller that had re-implemented a fragment of it.
Duplication collapses: fragments repeated across the monolith (or re-grown in every client) become one named operation with one meaning.
Discoverability improves: an operation is found where its concept lives, not in a *Service, *Helper or *Utils file chosen by guesswork.
The axes of change and stability become visible, giving refactoring a stable seam so later insight about the domain can be applied incrementally instead of as a rewrite.
tradeoffs: There is no mechanical rule for where the contour runs: the division is a domain judgment refined only by successive refactorings, so early contours are usually wrong (Evans calls the pattern intuitive and hard to explain).

Failure is symmetric and easy to overshoot: coarse units duplicate functionality and mix meanings, while over-fine units force every client to assemble the pieces and can lose the concept completely ('half of a uranium atom is not uranium').
Contours churn as understanding deepens: re-cutting a unit rewrites call sites, tests and persistence mappings, so each round of improved insight costs real refactoring effort.

It works against technical layering: ORMs (no-argument constructors, setters), serializers, generated code and framework lifecycles push behaviour out of the concept unit, and every exception needs an explicit decision.

A wrong contour is silent: it compiles and passes tests, and only shows up later as change effort - the pattern is a review and refactoring discipline, not a component whose effect can be measured directly.

Over-application costs discoverability: extension functions, free functions and mixins are not listed where the type is defined, so a model made of many tiny concept modules is harder to navigate than the monolith it replaced.

participants.responsibility: The class, interface, aggregate or module that owns exactly one domain concept - its state, invariants and operations - and hides its representation behind a narrow interface.
The small set of public operations that read as statements in the ubiquitous language and let clients combine behaviour without reaching for internals.
Composes the unit's operations to express use cases and never reassembles the concept from fragments or manipulates its state directly.

use_cases: Refactoring an anemic domain model: moving validation, calculation and state-transition methods from *Service classes onto the entity or aggregate that owns the state.
Cutting a god class or god module (Manager, Core, System) into units that each mirror a term of the ubiquitous language.
Merging scattered helpers (OrderValidator, OrderCalculator, OrderUtils) back into the concept they serve, or justifying why they are genuinely separate.
Deciding the physical layout of a codebase - which types and functions share a file, namespace, package or module - as part of model refinement rather than code style.
Reviewing a model before it ossifies: testing candidate divisions against the axes of change and stability observed in recent refactorings.

Decomposing a microservice or bounded context: applying conceptual contours to decide which domain concepts belong together vs. should be separated into distinct services, using the principle that concepts changing together for the same reason should share a contour.

Designing aggregates: using conceptual contours to decide which entities and value objects travel together inside an aggregate boundary, keeping strongly coupled concepts with high co-change rates co-located.
Structuring an event-driven model: placing commands, events and their handlers inside the concept unit that owns the state they operate on, rather than in a separate event-handling layer.

Making the contour architecturally evident in Java: jMolecules annotates the concept units themselves (@AggregateRoot, @Entity, @ValueObject, @Identity on domain-typed ids like IBAN on BankAccount) so the model's divisions are visible in code, and jQAssistant plugins or ArchUnit rules verify that aggregate boundaries and identifier types are actually honoured.

Modelling event-sourced aggregates in Axon Framework: the aggregate root carries command-handling methods that validate commands against current state and apply events, so the consistency boundary is also the unit that owns behaviour and emits domain events (@AggregateIdentifier, @CommandHandler, @EventSourcingHandler).

Letting persistence follow the contour in Spring Data JDBC: the aggregate root is the unit of load and save and every entity reachable from it belongs to that aggregate, so a well-cut contour needs no manual object-graph management while a mis-cut one shows up immediately as mapping pain.
avoid_when: A simple CRUD or transaction-script application: a table-driven data layer is simpler and a concept-centred decomposition buys nothing (a domain model is not always the best tool).
The behaviour is a genuine cross-cutting or utility concern (logging, time, configuration, serialization): it has no single owning concept, so a utility or service module is the honest home.
The shape is dictated by an external framework, schema generator or ORM that cannot tolerate encapsulated state - map at the boundary instead of fighting the tool inside the concept.
The team has no shared domain vocabulary or domain-expert access: without the language to name concepts, any division is technical and the pattern's premise fails.
anti_patterns: Anemic domain model: entities reduced to public getters and setters with all rules living in *Service classes (Fowler's anti-pattern).
God class or god module: one Manager/Core/System unit that mixes meanings, duplicates functionality and publishes an interface that hides what clients actually need.
Technical slicing: grouping by layer or mechanism (OrderService, OrderHelper, OrderValidator, OrderRepository), so one concept's rules sit in files that change together but never meet.
Contour by extension: scattering a single concept through extension methods, partial classes, monkey patches or reopened types, so the concept has no definition site.
Over-fragmentation: one-method classes and single-function modules that clients must assemble, losing the concept en route.
pitfalls: Cutting contours by team structure rather than domain concepts: if a concept spans teams, the contour boundary may reflect org chart seams rather than genuine domain divisions.

Treating contours as upfront architecture: Evans is explicit that conceptual contours emerge from refactoring and deeper insight; designing them upfront as a Big Bang usually produces technical slicing under a domain veneer.

Ignoring the cost of re-cutting: each contour change ripples through tests, persistence and call sites; teams that do not budget for this tend to freeze contours prematurely or avoid changing them even when the domain model has matured.

Mapping 1:1 from database tables to contours: persistence concerns introduce accidental coupling that widens contours beyond what the domain requires, creating anaemic entities backed by service-heavy designs.

Using the same contour grain for all bounded contexts: the same domain concept may have different contour granularity inside different bounded contexts; forcing a universal grain loses context-specific cohesion.

Wrong move: applying full concept-unit decomposition to a CRUD or transaction-script application, inventing aggregates, value objects and domain services for every table -> every simple change touches a trail of files and layers and the model obscures the business logic instead of expressing it -> instead start with transaction scripts and introduce concept units only where rules genuinely cohere and change together.

Wrong move: letting the ORM draw the contour - artificial ids, no-argument constructors and setters added to value objects so JPA can map them -> the objects degrade to entities and invariants leak into repositories and services -> instead translate at a persistence boundary or use an aggregate-aware store (Spring Data JDBC saves and loads the whole aggregate through its root) so the concept unit stays framework-free.

Wrong move: annotating anemic classes with DDD labels (@AggregateRoot, @ValueObject) and treating the labels as the design -> architecture checks pass over empty shells while behaviour still lives in *Service classes -> instead move the behaviour onto the unit first, then use annotations plus ArchUnit/jQAssistant rules to verify the contour the code already forms.
design_principles: High cohesion and low coupling: group what changes together and put the boundary where coupling is weakest.
Information hiding: a unit hides its design decisions behind an interface and exposes operations, not representation.
Separation of concerns along domain lines rather than technical layers.
Ubiquitous language: the model's names and divisions come from the domain vocabulary, not from the codebase's convenience.
Single responsibility: one concept, one reason to change, and understandable without reading the rest of the model.
best_practices: Put operations where their data is; when a method needs another unit's internals, move the method (or redesign the boundary) instead of adding getters.
Refactor in small steps and watch the axes of change and stability; do not freeze contours after one design session.
Name the unit with the domain term; if the name needs 'and' or more than a few words, it probably holds two concepts.
Keep the public interface a set of domain statements: prefer operations over attribute access, and constructors that establish invariants.
Use extension mechanisms (extensions, partials, mixins, extension traits) only for genuinely foreign or cross-cutting additions, and keep one concept's behaviour discoverable at its definition site.
Keep persistence, transport and framework concerns out of the concept's interface; translate at the boundary.
When reviewing a candidate contour, ask domain experts what operations make sense together; if they cannot name a coherent set, the boundary may be wrong.
Prefer coarser contours in early exploration and refine gradually; Evans describes contour design as iterative deepening of insight, not an initial blueprint.
Track change history: the concepts that change together for the same reason reveal their contours naturally over time; use recent refactorings as a map of where the real boundaries lie.
When merging multiple micro-concepts, verify the merged unit still has a coherent set of invariants; a false merge produces a god class in different clothing.
sources: Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software (2003) - Chapter 10 'Supple Design', CONCEPTUAL CONTOURS (p. 183).
Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design Reference (2015) - Second Edition with corrections and updates to the original text.
Vaughn Vernon, Implementing Domain-Driven Design (2013) - Chapters on aggregates, services and supple design patterns, with practical guidance on applying conceptual contours.

Michi Hausheer, 'DDD Concepts and Patterns – Supple Design 2', Opus Software AG blog (2019) - Practitioner treatment of conceptual contours and their relationship to cohesion, coupling and iterative refactoring.

Alberto Brandolini, EventStorming (2018) - Describes how event-based modelling surfaces conceptual boundaries and contours before code is written, providing a technique for discovering contours before implementation.
https://gist.github.com - 'DDD, CQRS & ES!' Gist summarizing Evans' conceptual contours in the context of bounded contexts and aggregates.

related_patterns_notes.module: A module is the physical packaging of a conceptual contour. A well-cut conceptual contour should map cleanly to one module; when it does not, that mismatch signals either a contour problem or a module problem.
related_patterns_notes.entity: Entities are almost always conceptual contours: they own identity, state and the operations that preserve invariants. The contour of an entity is the set of operations that are meaningless without its identity.
related_patterns_notes.value-object: Value objects are small, immutable conceptual contours where equality is based on attribute values. They demonstrate the principle at the finest grain: all behaviour and state that defines the concept are co-located and inseparable.
related_patterns_notes.aggregate: An aggregate defines a transactional contour: the cluster of entities and value objects that must be consistent together. Conceptual contours inside the aggregate should be finer-grained; the aggregate boundary itself is the outermost contour of that cluster.
related_patterns_notes.domain-service: A domain service holds operations that do not belong inside any single concept. Its existence is a signal that a conceptual contour may be missing or that two concepts genuinely intersect. Over-use of domain services is often a symptom of anemic contours.
related_patterns_notes.standalone-class: Standalone classes minimise external dependencies, making it easier to keep a conceptual contour internally cohesive and isolated. A conceptual contour should tend toward a standalone class when possible.
related_patterns_notes.closure-of-operations: Closure of operations describes a refined contour where an operation's arguments and return values are all of the same type, minimising coupling. This is the extreme end of the contour spectrum and is most valuable for mathematical or transformational concepts.
related_patterns_notes.intention-revealing-interface: Intention-revealing interface is the external face of a conceptual contour: a contour's public API should make the intent of an operation visible, not just its mechanism. Together they form the two halves of supple design: the internal division (contour) and the external communication (interface).
